chunks.title: PVD & retinal tears
chunks.tldr: PVD: new floaters, flashes, Weiss ring. 8–26% have a tear; tobacco dust (Shafer) or VH → >70% chance of a break. Always depressed indirect both eyes. No tear: review 4–6 weeks (2 weeks if punctate haemorrhages; 24 h by retina if VH/pigment). Tears: laser/cryo within 24 h for acute symptomatic horseshoe/operculated tears, traumatic breaks/dialysis, symptoms + lattice.
points: Consider treating asymptomatic breaks that are large, superior, in aphakes/pseudophakes, high myopes, or fellow eye of RD.
Dense VH → B-scan.
Mimics: vitritis (bilateral, non-pigmented cells), migraine aura.
Teach RD warning signs: more floaters/flashes, curtain, blur.
After laser: 2 wk, 6 wk, 3 mo, then 6–12-monthly.
chunks.hook: Pigment in the vitreous = hole in the retina.

cards.q: What is Shafer sign and its significance?
cards.a: Pigmented cells (tobacco dust) in the anterior vitreous — >70% chance of a retinal break with acute PVD.

cards.q: When to treat an acute symptomatic horseshoe tear?

chunks.title: Retinal detachment: three types
chunks.tldr: Rhegmatogenous: break + corrugated mobile retina, pigment cells; IOP low (or high in Schwartz–Matsuo). Chronic: demarcation line, cysts. Exudative: smooth, bullous, shifting fluid, no break (tumour, VKH, posterior scleritis, CSCR, Coats, malignant HTN, uveal effusion). Tractional: concave, immobile, membranes (PDR, sickle, ROP, PVR). Macula-on RRD → urgent surgery; macula-off within 7–10 days gives same outcome.
points: Repair: pneumatic retinopexy, scleral buckle, vitrectomy.
Exudative: treat the cause.
TRD: operate if macula threatened.
Post-op visits: day 1, week 1, month 1, 2–3 months.
chunks.hook: Macula on → operate today. Macula off → this week.

cards.q: Hallmark of exudative RD?
cards.a: Shifting subretinal fluid with position, no retinal break.

chunks.title: Retinoschisis
chunks.tldr: Age-related: bilateral, inferotemporal, smooth dome, snowflakes on inner wall, absolute scotoma, no pigment/haemorrhage, hyperopes; split at OPL. Treat only if a progressive RD develops. X-linked: boys, petaloid foveal schisis that doesn't leak on FA, peripheral schisis in 50%, VH; ERG: reduced b-wave (negative ERG); topical CAI may thin fovea; treat amblyopia.
points: RD vs schisis: RD corrugated, mobile, relative scotoma, demarcation line.
OCT shows the split layer.
Review 6-monthly; teach RD symptoms.
chunks.hook: Schisis = smooth, still, silent field (absolute scotoma).

cards.q: ERG finding in X-linked retinoschisis?
cards.a: Reduced b-wave with preserved a-wave (negative ERG).

chunks.title: Cotton-wool spots
chunks.tldr: Fluffy white NFL infarct (blocked axoplasmic flow). Even one is abnormal. Commonest: diabetes, hypertension, RVO. If none of these → work up: GCA, emboli, lupus and vasculitis, HIV, hypercoagulable states, radiation, Purtscher, leukaemia/mets, anaemia, interferon. Fade in 5–7 weeks.
points: Bloods: BP, glucose/HbA1c, ESR/CRP/platelets, HIV, CBC, ANA as indicated.
Mimics: infectious retinitis (vitritis!), myelinated nerve fibres.
chunks.hook: One CWS without DM/HTN/RVO = look for systemic disease.

cards.q: Isolated CWS in a non-diabetic normotensive patient — key tests?
cards.a: ESR/CRP (GCA if older), HIV, ANA/vasculitis screen, CBC, emboli workup.

chunks.title: CRAO & BRAO
chunks.tldr: Sudden painless loss (CF–LP), white retina + cherry-red spot, boxcarring, RAPD; cilioretinal sparing may save central vision. Treat as a stroke: send to ED/stroke centre now. Age ≥55 without embolus → ESR/CRP/platelets, steroids if GCA. Emboli: cholesterol (Hollenhorst, carotid), calcium (valves), platelet-fibrin. Workup: carotid duplex, ECG/echo, BP, bloods.
points: Unproven ocular Rx within 90–120 min: massage, paracentesis, acetazolamide/timolol.
LP or worse → think ophthalmic artery occlusion (no cherry-red spot; GCA).
NVI in up to 20% at ~4 weeks → review 1–4 weeks; PRP/anti-VEGF.
BRAO with disc oedema/retinitis → Bartonella, syphilis, Lyme, toxo.
Cherry-red spot mimics: Tay–Sachs, Niemann–Pick, commotio.
chunks.hook: Cherry-red spot = eye stroke → ED now, GCA bloods if old.

cards.q: Hollenhorst plaque — composition and source?
cards.a: Cholesterol embolus from carotid atheroma; refractile yellow at bifurcations.

cards.q: When does neovascularisation typically appear after CRAO?

chunks.title: Central retinal vein occlusion
chunks.tldr: Blood and thunder: haemorrhages in all 4 quadrants, dilated tortuous veins, disc oedema, CWS, ME. Risks: HTN (commonest systemic), glaucoma (commonest ocular), hypercoagulable, OCP, diuretics. Ischaemic: VA <20/200, RAPD, >10 DD non-perfusion → high NVI risk. Undilated gonio + iris check every visit. NVI/NVA → PRP promptly ± anti-VEGF. ME → anti-VEGF (ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab) or dexamethasone implant/triamcinolone 1 mg (SCORE).
points: Lower IOP in both eyes; stop OCP.
Young patients: thrombophilia screen, homocysteine, APL, syphilis, SPEP.
No prophylactic PRP unless follow-up unreliable.
Monthly visits initially.
Fellow eye RVO risk 8–10%.
OIS mimic: dilated but not tortuous veins, midperipheral blots, low IOP, pain.
chunks.hook: Blood and thunder fundus → check the angle every visit.

cards.q: Most common ocular association of CRVO?
SCORE-CRVO finding?
cards.a: Intravitreal triamcinolone 1 mg as effective as 4 mg with fewer side effects.

chunks.title: BRVO, hypertensive retinopathy & OIS
chunks.tldr: BRVO: sectoral haemorrhages at an AV crossing, respect the horizontal raphe; ME → anti-VEGF first-line (BRAVO), dex implant, focal laser (BVOS: oedema 3–6 mo + VA <20/40); NV → sector PRP. Hypertensive: arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, copper/silver wire; malignant: macular star, disc swelling, Elschnig spots → ≥180/110 or symptoms = ED. Unilateral? Carotid stenosis protecting the other eye. OIS: ≥90% carotid stenosis, men 50–80, NVI 66%, midperipheral blots, pain, slow light recovery → endarterectomy, PRP.
points: Aortic arch disease/Takayasu: bilateral OIS, absent pulses.
Secondary HTN: preeclampsia, phaeo, renal, coarctation.
chunks.hook: BRVO stops at the midline; diabetes doesn't.

cards.q: Fundus sign of past acute hypertensive choroidal infarcts?
Typical carotid stenosis in ocular ischaemic syndrome?

chunks.title: Diabetic retinopathy: staging
chunks.tldr: Mild NPDR: microaneurysms only. Moderate: more (CWS, beading). Severe NPDR = 4-2-1 rule: >20 haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2, IRMA in 1. PDR: any NV (disc, elsewhere, iris, angle) or VH/preretinal blood. DME at any stage — treat if centre-involving/threatening. Check iris and angle before dilating.
points: Follow-up: none → yearly; mild → 6–9 mo; moderate–severe → 4–6 mo; non-high-risk PDR → 2–3 mo.
DCCT: tight control slows retinopathy.
Pregnancy: mild–moderate NPDR → every trimester; severe/PDR → monthly; DME often regresses postpartum.
PDR mimics: sickle (sea fan), talc, sarcoid, RVO, OIS, radiation.
chunks.hook: 4-2-1: haemorrhages in 4, beading in 2, IRMA in 1 = severe.

cards.q: State the 4-2-1 rule.
cards.a: Severe NPDR: diffuse haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in ≥2, or IRMA in ≥1.

chunks.title: Diabetic retinopathy: treatment
chunks.tldr: Centre-involving DME → anti-VEGF first (ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab); poor responders → dexamethasone or fluocinolone implant/triamcinolone; focal laser for extrafoveal leaking MAs. PRP for high-risk PDR: NVD >¼–⅓ disc; any NVD + VH; NVE >½ disc + VH; any NVI/NVA. Anti-VEGF is an alternative (Protocol S) — but patients lost to follow-up do worse without PRP.
points: Vitrectomy: non-clearing VH, TRD involving macula, dense premacular blood, ERM/VMT, refractory DME, progressive fibrovascular proliferation.
Type 1 young diabetics: aggressive — consider earlier treatment.
Dense VH → B-scan for macular TRD.
Avoid anti-VEGF in pregnancy (most).
chunks.hook: Oedema → injections. High-risk NV → laser (unless they'll definitely come back).

cards.q: List the DRS high-risk characteristics.
cards.a: NVD ≥¼–⅓ DA; any NVD with VH/preretinal haemorrhage; NVE ≥½ DA with VH; (any NVI/NVA in Wills).

chunks.title: Vitreous haemorrhage
chunks.tldr: Sudden floaters/loss, no red reflex. Causes: PDR, PVD ± tear, RD, BRVO, wet AMD, sickle, trauma, Terson, tumour, macroaneurysm. Kids: abuse, XLRS, pars planitis. Check undilated iris, IOP, fellow eye; B-scan if no view. Observe: head up, no lifting, stop anticoagulants if possible; review daily for 2–3 days. Vitrectomy: RD/tear on US, non-clearing (⅔ idiopathic dense VH have a break/RD), NVI, ghost-cell glaucoma.
points: Inferior layered blood can mimic a break on B-scan.
Chronic VH looks yellow ochre.
chunks.hook: Unexplained dense VH = assume a tear until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Proportion of idiopathic fundus-obscuring VH with a retinal tear/RD?

chunks.title: Cystoid macular oedema
chunks.tldr: Blunted foveal reflex, cysts on OCT, petaloid leak on FA. Causes: post-op (Irvine–Gass, peaks 6–10 weeks), diabetes, RVO, uveitis (pars planitis), RP, PGA/epinephrine drops, vasculitis, ERM, AMD. Pseudo-CME (no leak): niacin, taxanes, XLRS, myopic schisis, Goldmann–Favre. Rx: topical NSAID + steroid → sub-Tenon/intravitreal steroid, anti-VEGF, oral acetazolamide (RP), YAG/vitrectomy for vitreous wick.
points: Gonio post-cataract: retained lens fragment, ACIOL haptic.
Angiographic CME without OCT change isn't treated.
chunks.hook: Post-cataract blur at 6 weeks = Irvine–Gass → NSAID + steroid drops.

cards.q: Peak onset of Irvine–Gass CME?

chunks.title: Central serous chorioretinopathy
chunks.tldr: Young–middle-aged men, type A, steroids (any route, incl. nasal/skin), pregnancy, Cushing. Blurry, dim, micropsia, metamorphopsia; dome of SRF, no blood/lipid. FA: smokestack (10–20%) or ink blot; EDI-OCT: thick choroid. Rx: stop steroids, observe (usually settles). Chronic/recurrent: half-dose PDT, laser to extrafoveal leak, eplerenone/spironolactone.
points: Review every 6–8 weeks.
Laser if >several months, recurrence with prior deficit, fellow eye damaged, or occupational need.
Watch for secondary CNV → anti-VEGF.
DDx: AMD, optic pit, PED, tumour, HTN.
chunks.hook: Stressed man on steroid cream with a blister at the macula = CSCR.

cards.q: Classic FA pattern in CSCR?

chunks.title: Dry AMD & AREDS
chunks.tldr: Drusen, pigment clumps, RPE atrophy, geographic atrophy; bilateral. AREDS for intermediate AMD (≥1 large druse ≥125 µm or ≥20 medium) or advanced AMD in one eye: ↓ progression ~25% over 5 years. AREDS2: vit C 500 mg, vit E 400 IU, lutein + zeaxanthin (replaces β-carotene), zinc 80 mg, copper 2 mg. No β-carotene in smokers (lung cancer).
points: Amsler grid/home monitoring daily; review 6–12 monthly.
Disappearing drusen may herald CNV.
Leafy greens (careful with warfarin), oily fish; stop smoking.
Low-vision aids.
DDx: myopic degeneration, CSCR, Stargardt/Best/pattern, chloroquine, inflammatory.
chunks.hook: AREDS2: swap β-carotene for lutein/zeaxanthin.

cards.q: Which AREDS component is contraindicated in smokers and why?

chunks.title: Wet AMD
chunks.tldr: Sudden distortion/scotoma; SRF, haemorrhage, exudate, PED from CNV. Types: Type 1 occult (sub-RPE), Type 2 classic (subretinal, lacy early FA), Type 3 RAP (intraretinal, hairpin loop). OCT for monitoring; FA/OCTA to confirm; ICGA for RAP/PCV. Rx: intravitreal anti-VEGF — ranibizumab (MARINA/ANCHOR ~40% gain ≥3 lines), aflibercept (VIEW, q8w), bevacizumab non-inferior (CATT), brolucizumab (HAWK/HARRIER). Regimens: monthly, PRN, treat-and-extend.
points: Fellow-eye CNV risk 10–12%/year.
Risks: age, smoking, family history, soft drusen, pigment clumps, HTN, blue eyes, hyperopia.
PDT and thermal laser now rarely used.
Warn about endophthalmitis/RD symptoms after injections.
chunks.hook: New distortion in an old eye with drusen → OCT today, injection this week.

cards.q: Which trial showed bevacizumab non-inferior to ranibizumab for wet AMD?

chunks.title: PCV & retinal arterial macroaneurysm
chunks.tldr: PCV: orange subretinal polyps, big haemorrhagic/serous PEDs, few drusen; Asian/African, women, HTN; ICGA = gold standard (branching network + polyps). Rx: anti-VEGF ± PDT (EVEREST II, PLANET); better prognosis than AMD. RAM: elderly hypertensive women, blood at multiple levels (sub-, intra-, pre-retinal) around a white spot on an artery, circinate exudate; ⅓ have RVO. Rx: observe; laser/anti-VEGF for macular exudate; vitrectomy or pneumatic displacement for submacular/sub-ILM blood.
points: Laser to RAM can occlude the distal artery.
Check BP and lipids.
chunks.hook: Blood in every layer around an artery = macroaneurysm.

cards.q: Best imaging test to diagnose polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy?

chunks.title: Sickle retinopathy & Valsalva
chunks.tldr: Sickle: peripheral non-perfusion → sea fan NV; salmon patch, iridescent spots, black sunbursts, angioid streaks, conjunctival comma vessels. HbSC worst (Sickledex may be negative → electrophoresis). Goldberg stages 1–5: occlusion, AV anastomoses, NV, VH, RD. NV may autoinfarct; PRP if VH. Valsalva: sub-ILM macular haemorrhage after straining/coughing → observe (YAG hyaloidotomy if needed).
points: No retinopathy: yearly; retinopathy: 3–6 monthly.
Sickle + hyphaema: avoid CAIs, low IOP threshold (see Ch3).
Sea fan DDx: sarcoid, talc, Eales, ROP, FEVR, CML.
chunks.hook: SC disease = Seriously Complicated retina.

cards.q: Which sickle genotype causes the most proliferative retinopathy?

chunks.title: Pathological myopia, angioid streaks, POHS
chunks.tldr: Pathological myopia (>−6 D, AL ≥26.5 mm): tilted disc, myopic crescent, staphyloma, lacquer cracks, Fuchs spots, myopic schisis, lattice/RD, CNV → anti-VEGF. Angioid streaks: Bruch breaks radiating from disc, peau d'orange; PEPSI = PXE (commonest), Ehlers–Danlos, Paget, Sickle, Idiopathic; CNV → anti-VEGF. POHS: Ohio–Mississippi valley; 2 of 3: punched-out histo spots, peripapillary atrophy, macular CNV; no vitritis; no antifungals — anti-VEGF (often fewer injections than AMD).
points: Myopia/angioid streaks: polycarbonate goggles for sport (choroidal rupture/bleed from minor trauma).
Myopic glaucoma: progression without myopia progression suggests real glaucoma.
Angioid streak workup: skin biopsy (PXE), alkaline phosphatase (Paget), Hb electrophoresis.
Multifocal choroiditis looks like POHS but has inflammation.
chunks.hook: Angioid streaks = PEPSI.

cards.q: Most common systemic association of angioid streaks?
Classic triad of presumed ocular histoplasmosis?
cards.a: Histo spots, peripapillary atrophy, macular CNV — with no vitritis.

chunks.title: Macular hole, VMT & ERM
chunks.tldr: Macular hole: older women, ~20/200, red round centre. Gass: 1 impending (yellow spot/ring), 2 small FT hole, 3 FT + cuff, no PVD, 4 FT + complete PVD. Watzke–Allen: broken slit line = true hole. Stage 1: observe (50% resolve). FT hole: PPV + ILM peel + gas, ideally within 6 months; cataract follows. Ocriplasmin rarely used. ERM: cellophane sheen → pucker, vessel distortion, pseudohole; after PVD, tears, surgery, uveitis; peel if vision reduced.
points: OCT classifies hole size and VMT.
Lamellar hole: not full thickness, no cuff.
Check the periphery for breaks in ERM/PVD.
Solar retinopathy can mimic a small hole.
chunks.hook: Broken line on Watzke = real hole → vitrectomy + peel + gas.

cards.q: Gass stage 4 macular hole?
cards.a: Full-thickness hole with complete posterior vitreous detachment.

chunks.title: Choroidal detachment
chunks.tldr: Smooth orange-brown lobular 360° elevations; ora visible without indentation. Serous: low IOP, transilluminates; from wound/bleb leak, overfiltration, cyclodialysis cleft, uveitis/scleritis, nanophthalmos, uveal effusion. Haemorrhagic: severe pain, high IOP, no transillumination; intra/post-op or spontaneous on anticoagulants. Rx: atropine, steroid, fix the leak/cleft; drain if flat AC, lens–cornea touch, or kissing choroidals with pain/IOP; haemorrhage drains best after liquefaction (7–10 days).
points: Melanoma: asymmetric, doesn't transilluminate — B-scan.
Seidel test and gonio for cleft.
chunks.hook: Low IOP + choroidals = look for the leak. High IOP + agony = blood.

cards.q: When is drainage of suprachoroidal haemorrhage most successful?

chunks.title: Retinitis pigmentosa
chunks.tldr: Night blindness + ring scotoma → tunnel. Triad: bone spicules, attenuated arterioles, waxy disc pallor; vitreous cells; CME, ERM, PSC cataract. ERG reduced/flat. AR commonest; AD mildest; XL worst (carriers: salt-and-pepper / tapetal reflex). Possible help: vitamin A 15,000 IU + lutein (non-smokers; check LFTs), CAIs for CME, retinal implants, gene therapy.
points: Mimics with RPE-level pigment: thioridazine (>800 mg/d), chlorpromazine, syphilis, rubella (normal ERG), resolved RD, trauma, ophthalmic artery occlusion.
Bietti crystalline dystrophy: corneal + retinal crystals.
Pigmented paravenous atrophy: pigment along veins, ERG often normal.
chunks.hook: Bone spicules + skinny arteries + waxy disc = RP.

cards.q: Which RP inheritance pattern is most severe?

chunks.title: Syndromic RP & LCA
chunks.tldr: Usher: RP + congenital deafness (AR; commonest deaf-blind). Bardet–Biedl: RP + obesity, polydactyly, hypogonadism, learning disability. Refsum: ↑phytanic acid, ataxia, neuropathy, ichthyosis, anosmia → low-phytanic diet. Abetalipoproteinaemia: acanthocytes, fat malabsorption → vitamins A, E, K. Kearns–Sayre: salt-and-pepper + CPEO + heart block. LCA: congenital blindness, nystagmus, oculodigital eye-poking, flat ERG, keratoconus; RPE65 → voretigene (Luxturna), first approved retinal gene therapy.
points: Batten: seizures, dementia.
Alström/Cockayne/Alport: hearing loss.
Zellweger: hypotonia, hepatomegaly.
chunks.hook: Treatable RP: Refsum (diet) and abetalipoproteinaemia (vitamins).

cards.q: Target gene of voretigene neparvovec?

chunks.title: Night blindness: gyrate, choroideremia, CSNB
chunks.tldr: Gyrate atrophy: AR, scalloped atrophy spreading from midperiphery, high myopia, PSC; ornithine 10–20× ↑ → arginine-restricted diet + B6. Choroideremia: XL males, total loss of RPE/choriocapillaris, no bone spicules; carriers have square pigment granules. Vitamin A deficiency: white dots + Bitot spots, dry eye. CSNB: stationary, paradoxical pupils; Oguchi = Mizuo phenomenon (golden sheen fades in dark). Commonest cause of poor night vision: undercorrected myopia.
points: Zinc deficiency impairs vitamin A metabolism.
chunks.hook: Gyrate: Gobble less arginine.

cards.q: What is the Mizuo phenomenon?
cards.a: Golden fundus sheen in light that disappears after dark adaptation — Oguchi disease (CSNB).

chunks.title: Cone dystrophy, Stargardt, Best
chunks.tldr: Cone dystrophy: photophobia, worse in bright light, poor colour, normal-looking fundus early → bull's eye; photopic/30 Hz flicker ERG reduced, rods normal. Stargardt (ABCA4, AR): child/young adult, vision worse than fundus looks (not a malingerer!), pisciform flecks, beaten-metal macula; FA dark/silent choroid; avoid vitamin A, UV protection. Best (BEST1, AD): egg-yolk lesion, normal ERG but abnormal EOG (Arden ratio ↓; carriers too); CNV in 20%; hyperopia/angle closure.
points: Adult-onset foveomacular (pattern) dystrophy: smaller yolks, PRPH2, age 30–50.
Fundus albipunctatus: white dots, stationary; retinitis punctata albescens: progressive.
chunks.hook: Best = Bad EOG, Egg yolk.

cards.q: Which electrophysiology test is diagnostic in Best disease?
cards.a: EOG (reduced light rise / Arden ratio) with normal ERG.

cards.q: Supplement to avoid in Stargardt disease?

chunks.title: Hydroxychloroquine toxicity
chunks.tldr: Bull's eye maculopathy, paracentral scotomas; often irreversible and can progress after stopping. Risk: HCQ >5 mg/kg real weight/day (chloroquine >2.3), >5 years, renal disease, tamoxifen, macular disease. Baseline exam in year 1; annual screening after 5 years (sooner if risks): 10-2 field + SD-OCT (flying saucer sign); Asians: 24-2/30-2 + wide OCT (pericentral pattern); mfERG, FAF.
points: DDx bull's eye: cone dystrophy, Stargardt, AMD, Batten.
Stop with prescriber if toxicity found.
chunks.hook: HCQ: 5 mg/kg, 5 years, then yearly 10-2 + OCT.

cards.q: Maximum safe hydroxychloroquine dose?
cards.a: ≤5 mg/kg real body weight per day.

chunks.title: Crystals, optic pit, solar retinopathy
chunks.tldr: Crystalline retinopathy: talc (IV drug users, intravascular, peripheral NV), tamoxifen (perimacular, ME; no routine screening), canthaxanthin (ring, tanning pills), methoxyflurane (oxalate), Bietti, MacTel type 2 (check diabetes), emboli. Optic pit: grey temporal disc depression; may cause serous macular detachment/schisis → observe or vitrectomy + gas ± temporal disc laser. Solar retinopathy: eclipse/sungazing, yellow → red foveal spot, OCT outer retinal gap; observe, usually improves.
points: Acquired pit in glaucoma = sign of progression.
chunks.hook: Shiny crystals in vessels of a drug user = talc.

cards.q: Optic pit macular complication?
cards.a: Serous macular detachment/schisis extending from the disc.

chunks.title: Choroidal nevus vs melanoma
chunks.tldr: Nevus: flat/<2 mm, drusen on top. Risk of transformation TFSOM-DIM ("To Find Small Ocular Melanoma Doing IMaging"): Thickness >2 mm, Fluid, Symptoms, Orange pigment, Melanoma hollow on US, DIaMeter >5 mm; ≥4 → >50% grow. Melanoma: dome/mushroom (Bruch break), SRF, orange pigment, low internal reflectivity + choroidal excavation on A/B-scan, double circulation. Rx: mostly plaque brachytherapy (+ anti-VEGF q4m to limit radiation retinopathy); enucleation if large. Mets → liver: LFTs 6-monthly, liver MRI yearly.
points: Nevus: review 3–4 months then 6–12 monthly; high-risk 3–6 monthly.
Pigmented mimics: CHRPE (flat, lacunae, halo), RPE hyperplasia, blood, melanocytoma, choroidal detachment.
Amelanotic mimics: haemangioma (red-orange), mets (cream, multifocal, breast/lung), osteoma (young women, calcified), posterior scleritis, lymphoma, sclerochoroidal calcification.
FNAB for genetics/prognosis.
chunks.hook: To Find Small Ocular Melanoma Doing IMaging.

cards.q: Ultrasound features of choroidal melanoma?
cards.a: Low–moderate internal reflectivity, choroidal excavation, collar-button/mushroom shape.

cards.q: Commonest site of uveal melanoma metastasis?
